title: Supervised, unsupervised, semi- and self-supervised setups
prompt: Which statements correctly describe learning setups?

options.text: Learning image classes from images paired with human-provided labels is supervised learning.
options.explanation: Supervised learning means every training example comes with a target provided from outside, here the human label, and the model learns the mapping from input to that target.

options.text: Clustering unlabeled images is supervised learning because it groups similar images.
options.explanation: Grouping images does not make a setup supervised: there are no target labels to learn from, so clustering is an unsupervised problem. The tempting reasoning confuses "producing groups" with "being given labels".

options.text: Using a small labeled set together with a larger unlabeled set is semi-supervised learning.
options.explanation: Semi-supervised learning is defined by combining a few labeled examples with many unlabeled ones, using the unlabeled data to improve what the labels alone could teach.

options.text: Self-supervised learning requires a human-provided target label for every example.
options.explanation: Self-supervised learning builds its targets from the data itself (e.g. predicting a masked part or the next token), so no human annotation is needed. Requiring human labels for every example describes supervised learning.

explanation: Learning setups are distinguished by where the training signal comes from. Supervised learning uses externally provided targets, unsupervised learning has none (clustering, density estimation), semi-supervised learning mixes a few labels with many unlabeled examples, and self-supervised learning manufactures its targets from the raw data. A task producing groups or representations is not supervised unless human-provided labels are part of the training data.

title: What generalization means
prompt: Which statements describe generalization in machine learning?

options.text: Memorizing every training example.
options.explanation: Memorization is fitting the training set, and a model can memorize it perfectly while failing on new inputs. It describes the opposite of what generalization is meant to achieve.

options.text: Making accurate predictions on unseen inputs.
options.explanation: Generalization is performance on previously unseen inputs drawn from the same target distribution as the training data.

options.text: Increasing the number of model parameters.
options.explanation: More parameters raise model capacity, which can help or hurt generalization (a huge model can overfit). Capacity is a property of the model, not a definition or guarantee of generalization.

options.text: Achieving zero training error regardless of performance on new data.
options.explanation: Zero training error says nothing about new data: an overfit model can have zero training error and poor test error. Generalization is judged on data the model has not been fitted to.

explanation: Generalization is about performance on data the model did not train on, so it must be measured on held-out inputs from the target distribution. Training error, memorization and parameter count all relate to the training set or to capacity, and none of them guarantees good behaviour on unseen data. Zero training error together with poor test error is the classic sign of overfitting.

title: Dilation and padding in two convolutions
prompt: Two convolutions receive an NCHW input of shape $(3, 4, 15, 19)$. Each has eight $3\times 3$ filters, stride 1, groups 1 and a bias per filter. Layer A uses dilation 1 and padding 1; layer B uses dilation 2 and padding 2 (per side). Which statements are correct?

options.text: The effective kernel footprint of layer B is $5\times 5$, while that of layer A is $3\times 3$.
options.explanation: The effective kernel width is $d(k-1)+1$. With $k=3$ this is $2\cdot 2+1=5$ for dilation 2 and $1\cdot 2+1=3$ for dilation 1.

options.text: Equal weights and biases guarantee identical outputs from A and B.
options.explanation: The two layers read different input positions (neighbours at distance 1 versus distance 2), so the same weights produce different values. Only the output shapes coincide, which is easy to mistake for equal outputs.

options.text: Both outputs have shape $(3, 8, 15, 19)$.
options.explanation: For $k=3$ and stride 1, $H_{out}=H+2p-d(k-1)=H+2p-2d$. Both layers have $p=d$, so height 15 and width 19 are preserved and the channels become 8.

options.text: Layer B has more trainable weights than layer A.
options.explanation: Dilation changes where the kernel samples the input, not how many weights it has. Each layer has $8\cdot 4\cdot 3\cdot 3=288$ weights plus 8 biases, 296 parameters in total.

explanation: Dilation spreads the kernel taps apart: the effective footprint is $d(k-1)+1$, but the number of weights stays $C_{out}\cdot C_{in}\cdot k\cdot k$. The output size is $H_{out}=\lfloor (H+2p-d(k-1)-1)/s\rfloor+1$, so with $k=3$, stride 1 and $p=d$ the spatial size is preserved. A larger receptive field at no extra parameter cost is the point of dilation, but it also means the layer computes a different function from the undilated one.

title: What a bias-free 1×1 convolution can compute
prompt: A bias-free $1\times 1$ convolution (stride 1, padding 0, groups 1) receives two channels $u$ and $v$. It must output $u + 2v$ and $u - 2v$ at each spatial position for any input. Which statements are correct?

options.text: With different weights, this layer can output $uv$ for every input.
options.explanation: A bias-free $1\times 1$ convolution outputs a weighted sum $w_1u+w_2v$, which is linear. Matching $uv$ at $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ forces $w_1=w_2=0$, but then the output at $(1,1)$ is 0, not 1.

options.text: Filters $(1, 2)$ and $(1, -2)$ implement the required mapping.
options.explanation: Filter $(1,2)$ computes $1\cdot u+2\cdot v=u+2v$ and filter $(1,-2)$ computes $u-2v$, at every spatial position.

options.text: The filter weights must vary with spatial position.
options.explanation: Convolution shares each filter's weights over all positions, and the requested mapping uses the same coefficients everywhere, so position-dependent weights are not needed.

options.text: Setting groups to 2 would still allow this mapping for every input.
options.explanation: With 2 input channels, 2 output channels and groups 2, each output channel sees only one input channel. Both requested outputs mix $u$ and $v$, so grouping makes them impossible.

explanation: A $1\times 1$ convolution applies the same learned linear map across channels at every pixel, so it can compute any fixed linear combination of the input channels but nothing nonlinear such as a product. Using groups restricts which input channels each output can see, reducing what can be represented. Here the target is a fixed linear map with matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}$, which a single ungrouped layer represents exactly.

title: Pooling and ReLU: does the order matter?
prompt:
Consider the window

$$X = \begin{bmatrix} -8 & 4 \\ -4 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$$

Pooling uses all four entries and ReLU acts element-wise. Which statements are correct?

options.text: Reversing the order of max pooling and ReLU changes the result.
options.explanation: ReLU is non-decreasing, so $\max_i \text{ReLU}(x_i)=\text{ReLU}(\max_i x_i)$. Both orders give 6; the order only matters for average pooling.

options.text: ReLU followed by average pooling gives 2.5.
options.explanation: ReLU turns the window into entries 0, 4, 0, 6, and their mean over all four positions is $(0+4+0+6)/4=2.5$.

options.text: Max pooling followed by ReLU gives 6.
options.explanation: The maximum of the original window is 6, and ReLU leaves a positive value unchanged, so the result is 6.

options.text: Average pooling followed by ReLU gives 2.5.
options.explanation: The original mean is $(-8+4-4+6)/4=-0.5$, and ReLU of that is 0. The value 2.5 belongs to the opposite order (ReLU first, then average).

explanation: Max pooling commutes with ReLU because ReLU is non-decreasing: both orders give 6. Average pooling does not commute with ReLU: averaging first gives $\max(0,-0.5)=0$, while clipping the negatives first gives $(0+4+0+6)/4=2.5$. In the second order the zeros created by ReLU still count in the denominator, whereas the negative values pull the mean down in the first order.

title: Parameters of a linear classifier on flattened images
prompt: A linear classifier takes flattened RGB images of size $16\times 16$ and predicts one of 5 classes. It computes $S = XW + b$, with $W$ of shape $(D, 5)$ and one trainable bias per class. Compute the total number of trainable scalar parameters.
hints: First find D, the length of one flattened image; RGB has three channels.
Add the number of bias entries to the number of weight-matrix entries.
explanation: RGB has 3 channels, so $D = 3\cdot 16\cdot 16 = 768$. The weight matrix has $768\cdot 5 = 3840$ entries and there are 5 biases, so $$768\cdot 5 + 5 = 3845$$ An equivalent form is $(3\cdot16\cdot16+1)\cdot 5$. Typical wrong results: forgetting the bias gives 3840; using a single grayscale channel ($D=256$) gives $256\cdot5+5=1285$; multiplying by the batch size is wrong because the batch size never adds trainable parameters.

title: in_features and total parameters of a small CNN
prompt: Input shape: $(N, 3, 10, 12)$. Convolutions use stride 1, dilation 1 and groups 1. Find the missing in_features of the final linear layer, then count the trainable parameters of the whole model.
code:
import torch.nn as nn
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(3, 4, 3, padding=1, bias=True), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool2d(2, stride=2),
    nn.Conv2d(4, 5, 1, bias=False), nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(____, 6, bias=True),
)
hints: Track the tensor shape through every layer, one at a time.
ReLU, pooling and flatten have no trainable parameters; the 1×1 convolution has no bias.
explanation:
Shapes: $(N,3,10,12)$ goes through the 3×3 convolution with padding 1, which keeps the spatial size: $(N,4,10,12)$. Max-pooling 2×2 with stride 2 halves it: $(N,4,5,6)$. The 1×1 convolution gives $(N,5,5,6)$ and flatten gives $(N,150)$, so in_features $=5\cdot5\cdot6=150$.

Parameters: first convolution $4\cdot(3\cdot3\cdot3+1)=112$; second convolution has no bias, $5\cdot4\cdot1\cdot1=20$; linear layer $150\cdot6+6=906$. Total $112+20+906=1038$. Typical mistakes: adding a bias to the second convolution (+5 gives 1043), forgetting the first convolution's bias (-4), or forgetting to halve the spatial size at pooling (in_features 600).

title: Per-channel normalization with broadcasting
description: Normalizes an image batch channel by channel: each channel's mean is subtracted and the result is divided by that channel's standard deviation. The statistics are reshaped so they broadcast against the batch, and the function returns the normalized tensor.
code:
import torch

def normalize_channels(x: torch.Tensor, mean: torch.Tensor, std: torch.Tensor):
    # x: (B, C, H, W), mean: (C,), std: (C,), std > 0
    mean_bc = mean.reshape(1, -1, 1, 1)
    std_bc = std.reshape(1, -1, 1, 1)

    <<BLANK:ret>>
hints: mean_bc and std_bc have shape (1, C, 1, 1), so ordinary arithmetic broadcasts them over batch and spatial positions.
The line must hand the result back to the caller, not just compute it.
explanation: The reshaped statistics have shape $(1, C, 1, 1)$, so broadcasting applies each channel's own mean and standard deviation to every image and every spatial position: $y_{b,c,h,w}=(x_{b,c,h,w}-\text{mean}_c)/\text{std}_c$. The output keeps shape $(B,C,H,W)$ and positive standard deviations make the division safe. Without `return`, the expression is computed and thrown away and the function returns `None`; using the unreshaped `mean` and `std` of shape $(C,)$ would try to broadcast against the last axis $W$ instead of the channel axis.

title: Per-channel 3×3 max pooling with stride 3
description: Performs per-channel 3x3 max pooling with stride 3 and no padding on an NCHW tensor. It loops over output positions, takes the non-overlapping window for each, and stores one maximum per batch item and channel. Exactly two lines are faulty.

errors.explanation: The window starts at (i, j), so consecutive output positions slide by one input pixel (stride 1) and overlap. With stride 3 the window for output (i, j) must start at (3i, 3j) in both spatial directions.

Reducing over dim=(1, 2, 3) includes the channel axis, so every channel receives the maximum over all channels. Only the spatial axes 2 and 3 should be reduced, giving shape (N, C) directly; the extra [:, None] must be removed as well, otherwise it only worked by accident through broadcasting.

hints: Which input pixel should the window for output position (i, j) start at when the stride is 3?
Which axis of an NCHW tensor is the channel axis, and should a per-channel pool reduce over it?
explanation: Max pooling with kernel 3 and stride 3 uses non-overlapping windows starting at (3i, 3j), and it must reduce only over the two spatial axes so each channel is pooled independently. The first fault (window start at (i, j)) gives overlapping windows that move one pixel per step; the second fault (reducing axis 1 too) mixes channels, and the trailing [:, None] only hides the shape mismatch through broadcasting. After the fix, `window.amax(dim=(2, 3))` already has shape (N, C), matching `out[:, :, i, j]`.

title: Why generalization is not measured on the training set
prompt: A model reaches zero training error. Explain why this does not tell you that it generalizes well, and how you would actually assess generalization.
model_answer: Generalization means accurate predictions on unseen inputs from the target distribution. A flexible model can memorize the training examples, including their noise, and so reach zero training error while performing poorly on new data. Training error is measured on the data the model was fitted to, so it is an optimistic estimate. To assess generalization you evaluate on held-out data (validation or test set) not used for fitting.
key_points: Generalization is about performance on unseen inputs from the target distribution.
A model can memorize the training set (including noise) and get zero training error but fail on new data.
Training error is measured on fitted data and is therefore an optimistic estimate.
It is assessed with held-out validation or test data.
hints: What would a lookup table of the training examples score on the training set and on new data?
Where must the data come from to judge performance on inputs the model has not seen?
explanation: The key idea is that fitting the training data and generalizing are different goals. A high-capacity model can interpolate the training set, noise included, which shows up as a large gap between training and test error (overfitting). Common half-answers only say that more parameters cause overfitting, which is not the explanation: it is the gap between performance on fitted data and unseen data that matters, and the remedy for measuring it is held-out evaluation.

title: Dilation: more context without more parameters
prompt: A $3\times 3$ convolution with dilation 2 has the same number of parameters as one with dilation 1. Explain what dilation changes, how it affects the output size, and why equal weights do not give equal outputs.
model_answer: Dilation spaces the kernel taps apart, so a $3\times 3$ kernel with dilation $d$ covers an effective footprint of $d(k-1)+1$, i.e. $5\times 5$ for $d=2$. The number of weights is still $C_{out}C_{in}k^2$, because only the sampling positions change. Since the footprint shrinks the output by $d(k-1)$ per axis, padding $p=d$ is needed to preserve the size. With the same weights the layers read different pixels, so their outputs differ.
key_points: Dilation spaces the kernel taps apart, giving effective width $d(k-1)+1$.
The parameter count is unchanged because only sampling locations change.
The output size follows $H+2p-d(k-1)$ (stride 1), so $p=d$ preserves size for $k=3$.
Different sampled positions mean the same weights produce different outputs.
hints: Compare which input pixels each tap reads for dilation 1 and dilation 2.
Count the weights: does the formula for the weight count contain d?
explanation: Dilation enlarges the receptive field cheaply: the kernel still has $k\times k$ taps, but they are spread over a larger area. That is why the weight count and output-shape arithmetic (through the effective kernel size) behave differently. A common mistake is saying dilation adds parameters or that layers with equal shapes and weights compute the same function; the shapes match only because the padding was chosen to compensate.

title: Why pooling and ReLU commute only for max pooling
prompt: Explain why max pooling followed by ReLU gives the same result as ReLU followed by max pooling, but average pooling does not.
model_answer: ReLU is non-decreasing, so the largest input maps to the largest output: $\max_i \text{ReLU}(x_i)=\text{ReLU}(\max_i x_i)$, and both orders of max pooling and ReLU agree. Averaging is different: the mean of ReLU outputs is not the ReLU of the mean, because ReLU is nonlinear. Clipping negatives first raises the mean, whereas averaging first lets negative values pull the mean down before the clip, so the results can differ.
key_points: ReLU is non-decreasing, so it preserves which entry is the maximum.
Therefore max pooling and ReLU commute.
ReLU is nonlinear, so the mean of ReLU outputs differs from the ReLU of the mean.
Example: with entries -8, 4, -4, 6 the orders give 2.5 and 0.
hints: What happens to the position of the largest entry after applying a non-decreasing function?
Try the window with entries -8, 4, -4, 6 in both orders for average pooling.
explanation: The argument rests on two properties: ReLU is monotone (so it commutes with max) and nonlinear (so it does not commute with averaging). For $X$ with entries $-8, 4, -4, 6$, ReLU then average gives $(0+4+0+6)/4=2.5$, while average then ReLU gives $\max(0,-0.5)=0$. A frequent half-answer is to say that average pooling "uses all entries"; the crucial point is that ReLU does not commute with a linear average of entries of mixed sign.

title: Linearity limits of a 1×1 convolution
prompt: A bias-free $1\times 1$ convolution (stride 1, padding 0, groups 1) receives channels $u$ and $v$. Explain why it can output $u+2v$ but never $uv$ for every input, and what changes if groups is set to 2.
model_answer: A bias-free $1\times 1$ convolution computes a weighted sum $w_1u+w_2v$ at every position, which is linear in the channels, and $u+2v$ is exactly such a sum with weights $(1,2)$. The product $uv$ is not linear: matching it at $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ forces both weights to zero, which then fails at $(1,1)$. With groups 2 and two channels each output sees only one input channel, so it can no longer mix $u$ and $v$, and $u+2v$ becomes impossible.
key_points: A bias-free 1×1 convolution is a linear map across channels at each position.
u+2v is a fixed weighted sum, so weights (1, 2) realize it.
uv is not linear; the checks at (1,0), (0,1), (1,1) show no weights work.
With groups 2 each output sees only one input channel, so channels cannot be mixed.
hints: What kind of function of (u, v) can a weighted sum represent?
With groups = 2 and two input channels, how many input channels does each filter see?
explanation: The 1×1 convolution is a per-pixel matrix multiplication across channels, so it can only express linear combinations of the inputs. Multiplying features requires a nonlinearity (or a bilinear or attention-style layer). Grouping splits the channels into independent blocks, so with groups equal to the channel count each output depends on exactly one input channel. A usual mistake is to think that choosing the weights cleverly can create a product, or that position-dependent weights are needed.

title: Why reshape statistics to (1, C, 1, 1)
prompt: In per-channel normalization of a tensor of shape $(B, C, H, W)$ with per-channel mean and std of shape $(C,)$, explain why the statistics are reshaped to $(1, C, 1, 1)$ before the subtraction and division.
model_answer: Broadcasting aligns shapes from the trailing axis, so a vector of shape $(C,)$ would be matched with the last axis $W$ instead of the channel axis and either fail or normalize the wrong dimension. Reshaping to $(1, C, 1, 1)$ puts the channel values on axis 1 and size-1 axes elsewhere, which broadcast over batch, height and width. Each channel is thus shifted and scaled by its own statistics with no loops.
key_points: Broadcasting aligns shapes starting from the last axis.
A (C,) vector would line up with W, not with the channel axis.
Shape (1, C, 1, 1) places the statistics on axis 1 and broadcasts over the others.
This normalizes every channel with its own mean and std without loops.
hints: Which axis of (B, C, H, W) does a tensor of shape (C,) get matched to under the broadcasting rules?
What does a size-1 axis do during broadcasting?
explanation: PyTorch broadcasting compares shapes from the right, so the axis meaning is determined by position, not by names. Reshaping to $(1, C, 1, 1)$ is how you tell the framework that the values belong to the channel axis. A common mistake is to assume that a $(C,)$ vector automatically applies per channel; it only works by coincidence when $C = W$, and then it normalizes the wrong axis.
